title: Mission to the Ice Moon
summary: A girl astronaut and her robot travel to an ice moon to find out where a faraway, very soft sound is coming from.

scenes.text:
Lía was seven years old, with a helmet that had her name painted on it and a dream as big as the sky.

In the training room, they played her a very short recording. It was a faraway, very soft sound, coming from Crystal: an ice moon that went round and round a giant planet, very, very far away.

Nobody knew what it was.

"Someone has to go and listen to it up close," said the scientists.

"I'll go," said Lía. And she said it so fast that her words got there before her heart did.

From that day on she trained every morning. She swam in her spacesuit in an enormous pool. She learned to move slowly. She learned to calm down when her heart started racing.

And always by her side was Chispa, her robot: the size of a dog, with wide wheels, an antenna and a blue light on his forehead.

On the last night before the journey, Lía had dinner at home.

Her grandma made soup and didn't say much, but she squeezed Lía's hand very tight. Her dad gave her a little photo of the three of them, the size of a biscuit, to carry in the pocket of her suit.

And her mum whispered in her ear:

"Listen carefully, my love. And come back."

At dawn, Lía climbed a very long staircase to the top of the spaceship, white and enormous like a tower. She hugged her family once, twice, three times.

Then she went inside. And behind her, slowly, closed the door.

Lía lay back in her seat and fastened her straps. A calm voice began to count backwards.

"Ten. Nine. Eight…"

With every number, the floor shook a little more.

"Three. Two. One…"

And then: blastoff!

It was a roar that started underneath her and climbed up her back all the way to her teeth. Lía felt an invisible hand pressing on her chest, and she smiled, just as she had practised so many times.

Through the little window, the world grew smaller. The sky went from blue to dark blue, and from dark blue to black with bright dots.

And suddenly, silence.

Lía opened her eyes. Her hair was floating, softly, like seaweed in the water.

"We're up," said Chispa.

Floating was the best thing in the world.

Lía learned to push off with one finger and glide the whole length of the ship. She learned to drink water from a bag with a little tube. She learned to leave her pencil still in the air and find it right there when she needed it.

She stuck the photo of her family next to the window. Outside, the Earth was a blue marble, a little smaller every day.

"Chispa, are we there yet?"

"Nineteen days to go."

"What about now?"

"Nineteen days and six seconds to go."

Lía got such a fit of the giggles that she had to grab a handle so she wouldn't go spinning off.

Then came the long days. The very long days.

In space it doesn't rain, it doesn't get dark, nobody walks down the street. Lía exercised with stretchy bands. She drew the ice moon twenty times. She played cards with Chispa, who always won and always announced: "I won again."

And she listened to the recording of the mysterious sound over and over again.

"It sounds like someone singing very far away," she would say.

"It sounds like ice moving," Chispa would say.

Some nights, Lía missed her bed so much that her chest ached. Then she would climb into her sleeping bag, which hung on the wall like a cocoon, and put the photo over her heart.

And after a little while, in the middle of all that silence, out would come a little snore.

On the nineteenth day, Chispa woke her early.

"Lía. Look out of the window."

There was Crystal. It wasn't a dot in a drawing any more: it was an enormous moon, round and bluish-white, with fine lines across it like the veins of a leaf.

Behind it, the giant planet filled half the window: blue and green, with swirls of cloud.

Lía rested her hand on the cold glass, slowly, the way you say hello to an animal you don't know yet.

"Hello," she said softly. "We've come to listen to you."

Landing wasn't easy. Crystal has no air, so they had to slow down with the engines, and the ground was full of cracks and mountains of ice.

"Zone one: too many cracks," said Chispa. "Zone two: mountains. Zone three… might do."

"Let's go for three."

The ship came down sideways, straightened up and hovered for a moment over a shining plain. Ice dust rose up like a white cloud.

And the legs touched the ground with a thump.

Everything in the cabin jumped. Then, silence.

"Are we in one piece?" asked Lía.

"We're in one piece," said Chispa. "And a tiny bit crooked."

Lía put on her suit slowly, checking every fastening twice, just like in training. The hatch opened, and she went down the little ladder very carefully.

The ice was blue. Really blue, blue like glass, with little white bubbles trapped inside, like sleeping stars.

Every time she put a boot down, the ground gave a crunch.

Above her, the giant planet hung enormous and silent. There was no wind. There were no birds. Just a silence so big that Lía could hear herself breathing inside her helmet.

They walked together towards the spot marked on the map. Chispa drew a line with his wheels as he went. And under their boots, far, far below, something enormous was keeping a secret.

The cold on Crystal isn't ordinary cold. It's a cold that bites metal.

After twenty minutes of walking, Chispa started talking strangely.

"Lía… the tempera… ture…"

His blue light flickered twice. And went out.

The robot stood still in the middle of the ice, his wheels twisted.

"Chispa. Chispa, answer me."

Nothing.

For the first time on the whole journey, Lía felt like crying. She was alone, further from home than anyone had ever been, and her only friend was switched off at her feet.

She remembered her mum: listen carefully, and come back. And then she did what she had learned in the pool.

Breathe.

Very deeply. Very slowly.

Lía opened her backpack and took out the toolbox. Her gloves were thick and her hands were shaking. So the first thing she did was keep very still, until her fingers would do as they were told.

"Right, Chispa," she said out loud, so she wouldn't feel so alone. "Let's see what's wrong with you."

She opened the panel on his back. Inside, one part was covered in frost, as white as sugar.

She cleaned it with a cloth, very, very carefully. She wrapped a thermal blanket around it. She tightened two screws the cold had loosened. And she swapped the battery for the spare one she kept in her pocket, next to the photo.

She counted to ten.

And slowly, like a star, the blue light glowed.

"Repor… reporting," said Chispa. "I'm all right. Thank you, Lía."

To hear what was underneath, they had to make a hole in the ice. A very thin hole, like a piece of spaghetti.

Lía set up the drill and started it. It turned slowly, very slowly. One centimetre. Two. Ten.

"No hurrying," Chispa kept saying. "If we hurry, the ice will crack."

"No hurrying," Lía would answer.

It took hours. Lía's arms ached, and her eyes shone.

Until, all of a sudden, the drill sank through.

And out of the hole came a little spurt of water, which froze in the air into tiny, shining beads.

They lowered a microphone down the hole on a thin cable. Lía sat on the ice with her knees against her chest and put on her headphones.

At first there was only a murmur, like a seashell held to your ear.

Then came the songs.

Lots and lots of voices.

Under the ice there was a whole ocean, deeper than all the seas on Earth put together. And it was full of voices. Some were deep and very long. Others sounded like drops, like bells. They called to each other, answered each other, crossed over and began again.

Lía sat with her mouth open and her eyes full of tears.

"Chispa," she whispered. "It isn't ice moving."

"No," said the robot, his blue light trembling. "They're singing."

In her backpack, Lía had a powerful torch and a camera she could lower down the hole. She could send them down. She could look.

She sat thinking for a long time, listening.

"If we shine a light in, they'll be frightened," she said at last. "Today we're only going to listen. And record. Nothing else."

She recorded for three whole hours. Then she covered the hole with snow, very gently, the way you tuck in someone who's asleep.

The journey home was peaceful. Lía listened to the recording every day. She gave the voices names: the One Who Always Answers, the Deep One, the Bell. And in her notebook, in big letters, she wrote:

"Under the ice there is a sea full of singing. We didn't disturb it."

On the last night before they arrived, Lía climbed into her sleeping bag with the voices playing very softly. Outside, the Earth was slowly growing, blue and warm.

And Lía fell asleep hugging a song that nobody had ever heard before.
